{{about|manifolds whose transition maps are affine transformations|manifolds embedded in an real affine space|Embedding#Differential topology}}
In [[differential geometry]], an '''affine manifold''' is a [[differentiable manifold]] equipped with a [[flat connection|flat]], [[torsion tensor|torsion-free]] [[affine connection|connection]].

Equivalently, it is a manifold that is (if connected) [[covering space|covered]] by an open subset of <math>{\mathbb R}^n</math>, with [[monodromy]] acting by [[affine transformation]]s. This equivalence is an easy corollary of [[Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks theorem]].

Equivalently, it is a manifold equipped with an atlas—called '''the affine structure'''—such that all transition functions between [[Chart (topology)|charts]] are [[affine transformation]]s (that is, have constant Jacobian matrix);{{sfn|Bishop|Goldberg|1968|pp=223–224}} two atlases are equivalent if the manifold admits an atlas subjugated to both, with transitions from both atlases to a smaller atlas being affine. A manifold having a distinguished affine structure is called an '''affine manifold''' and the charts which are affinely related to those of the affine structure are called '''affine charts'''. In each affine coordinate domain the coordinate [[vector field]]s form a [[parallelization (mathematics)|parallelisation]] of that domain, so there is an associated connection on each domain. These locally defined connections are the same on overlapping parts, so there is a unique connection associated with an affine structure. Note there is a link between [[linear]] [[connection (mathematics)|connection]] (also called [[affine connection]]) and a [[web (differential geometry)|web]].

==Formal definition==
An '''affine manifold''' <math>M\,</math> is a real [[manifold]] with charts <math>\psi_i\colon U_i\to{\mathbb R}^n</math> such that <math>\psi_i\circ\psi_j^{-1}\in \operatorname{Aff}({\mathbb R}^n)</math> for all <math>i, j\, ,</math> where <math>\operatorname{Aff}({\mathbb R}^n)</math> denotes the [[group (mathematics)|group]] of [[affine transformation]]s. In fancier words it is a [[(G,X)-manifold]] where <math>X=\mathbb R^n</math> and <math>G</math> is the group of affine transformations.

An affine manifold is called '''complete''' if its [[universal covering]] is [[homeomorphic]] to <math>{\mathbb R}^n</math>.

In the case of a compact affine manifold <math>M</math>, let <math>G</math> be the [[fundamental group]] of <math>M</math> and <math>\widetilde M</math> be its [[universal cover]]. One can show that each <math>n</math>-dimensional affine manifold comes with a developing map <math>D\colon {\widetilde M}\to{\mathbb R}^n</math>, and a [[homomorphism]] <math>\varphi\colon G\to \operatorname{Aff}({\mathbb R}^n)</math>, such that <math>D</math> is an [[immersion (mathematics)|immersion]] and equivariant with respect to <math>\varphi</math>.

A [[fundamental group]] of a compact complete flat affine manifold is called '''an affine [[crystallographic group]]'''. Classification of affine crystallographic groups is a difficult problem, far from being solved. The [[Space group|Riemannian crystallographic groups]] (also known as [[Bieberbach group]]s) were classified by [[Ludwig Bieberbach]], answering a question posed by [[David Hilbert]]. In his work on [[Hilbert's eighteenth problem|Hilbert's 18-th problem]], [[Space group#Bieberbach's theorems|Bieberbach proved]] that any Riemannian crystallographic group contains an abelian subgroup of finite index.

=== Complex affine manifolds ===

An ''affine complex manifold''  is a [[complex manifold]] that has an atlas whose [[transition map]]s belong to the group of complex [[affine transformations]], that is, have the form <math> z \mapsto A \cdot z + c</math> where <math>n</math> is the (complex) dimension of the manifold, <math>c\in \mathbb C^n,</math> and <math>A</math> is an invertible <math> n \times n </math> matrix with complex entries.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Fried | first1=Davis
| last2=Goldman | first2=William M.
| last3=Hirsch | first3=Morris
| title=Affine manifolds with nilpotent holonomy
| journal=[[Comment. Math. Helv.]]
| volume=56
| issue=4
| date=1981
| pages=487-523
| doi=10.1007/bf02566225| doi-access=free}}</ref>  In other words, it is a {{tmath|(G, X)}}-manifold where <math>X=\C^n</math> and <math>G</math> is the group of complex affine transformations of <math>\C^n.</math>

==Important longstanding conjectures==
Geometry of affine manifolds is essentially a network of longstanding conjectures; most of them proven in low dimension and some other special cases.

The most important of them are:

*Markus conjecture (1962) stating that a compact affine manifold is complete [[if and only if]] it has parallel volume. Known in dimension 2.
*Auslander conjecture (1964)<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Auslander | first1=Louis | title=The structure of locally complete affine manifolds | journal=Topology | volume=3 | issue=Supplement 1 | date=1964 | pages=131–139 | doi=10.1016/0040-9383(64)90012-6 | doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fried | first1=Davis | last2=Goldman | first2=William M. | title=Three dimensional affine crystallographic groups | journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] | volume=47 | issue=1 | date=1983 | pages=1–49 | doi=10.1016/0001-8708(83)90053-1 | doi-access=free}}</ref> stating that any affine crystallographic group contains a [[polycyclic group|polycyclic subgroup]] of finite [[Index of a subgroup|index]]. Known in dimensions up to 6,<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Abels | first1=Herbert | last2=Margulis | first2=Grigori A. | last3=Soifer | first3=Grigori A. | title=On the Zariski closure of the linear part of a properly discontinuous group of affine transformations | journal=Journal of Differential Geometry | volume=60 | date=2002 | issue=2 | pages=315–344 | doi=10.4310/jdg/1090351104 | doi-access=free}}</ref> and when the [[holonomy]] of the flat connection preserves a [[Lorentz metric]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Goldman | first1=William M. | last2=Kamishima | first2=Yoshinobu | title=The fundamental group of a compact flat Lorentz space form is virtually polycyclic | journal=Journal of Differential Geometry | volume=19 | issue=1 | pages=233–240 | date=1984 | doi=10.4310/jdg/1214438430 | doi-access=free}}</ref> Since every virtually polycyclic crystallographic group preserves a [[volume form]], Auslander conjecture implies the "only if" part of the Markus conjecture.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Abels | first1=Herbert | title=Properly Discontinuous Groups of Affine Transformations: A Survey | journal=[[Geometriae Dedicata]] | volume=87 | pages=309–333 | date=2001 | doi=10.1023/A:1012019004745 | doi-access=free}}</ref>
*[[Chern conjecture (affine geometry)|Chern conjecture]] (1955) The [[Euler class]] of an affine manifold vanishes.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Kostant | first1=Bertram | authorlink1=Bertram Kostant | last2=Sullivan | first2= Dennis | title=The Euler characteristic of an affine space form is zero | journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society | volume=81 | date=1975 | issue=5 | pages=937–938 | doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1975-13896-1 | doi-access=free}}</ref>
